text: This chapter has been building toward one moment: does an IOC earn its way into a live detection rule, or doesn't it. Everything from the normalization in Lesson 13 through the scoring pass in Lesson 15 exists to answer that question honestly, and this final lesson closes the loop by actually acting on the answer.

The gate is simple to state: only IOCs tagged auto_promote are eligible, full stop. Writing that as its own named function instead of inlining the condition means nobody can quietly wire a raw, unscored feed pull straight into production later without it being obvious in a code review. Promoted entries get pushed into the watchlist carrying their own expiration date, and a separate pruning job removes anything that's aged past it.

Pushing validated IOCs reuses the same bulk watchlist upsert pattern from Lesson 14, now scoped down to just the promotable set, with each entry tagged with where it came from, when it was promoted, and when it expires. That expiration field isn't decoration — without it, a promoted-IOC watchlist only ever grows, and a detection rule leaning on thousands of indicators from long-dead infrastructure becomes its own kind of noise problem.

The watchlist only matters once a live analytics rule actually joins against it, and the key design choice is that the rule references it by name rather than embedding a static list. That means updating the watchlist through this Python pipeline is enough to change what the rule fires on — nobody ever has to touch or redeploy the rule itself just to pick up newly promoted intel.

Put together, the whole chapter composes into one scheduled job: pull every feed, normalize it, dedupe across sources, check it against your own logs, score and tier it, promote what earned it, and prune what's no longer current. That's the full threat intelligence automation loop this chapter set out to build, running on its own schedule without anyone babysitting it.
